routes.description: Establish that early Christian sources report a transformed but physically continuous risen Jesus and that their cumulative historical provenance supports occurrence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony is historically usable, bodily in meaning, and better explained by Jesus having physically risen than by the proposed alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically grounded early testimony about Jesus after death to the conclusion that the body that died was raised in transformed physical continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and other early Christian testimony preserves resurrection claims sufficiently early and coherently to bear historical weight.
Show that spiritual and glorious body language denotes transformed embodiment rather than an immaterial survival or apparition.
Connect reported appearances and geographically dispersed early teaching to identifiable witnesses or apostolic transmission.
Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan analogues and account for costly early proclamation without dissolving it into ordinary legend.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use costly adherence and continued proclamation to support the sincerity and claimed eyewitness grounding of the resurrection belief.
Treat convergence among distinct early sources and communities as support for a common antecedent resurrection tradition.

routes.description: Withhold the bodily-resurrection conclusion by applying ordinary historical analogy and challenging the meaning, provenance, and independence of the Christian testimony.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources do not historically distinguish a bodily resurrection from spiritual interpretation, legendary transmission, inherited ideology, or comparable religious narratives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant inferring an actual bodily return from death under provisional, analogy-based historical inquiry.

centralBridges.description: Apply comparison with ordinary experience and ancient religious narratives when judging the probability of an extraordinary resurrection report.
Show that Pauline flesh, spirit, and spiritual-body language does not require physical continuity with Jesus's dead body.
Challenge the authorship, consistency, independence, and apostolic pedigree of the documents and transmission chains offered as evidence.
Provide nonmiraculous explanations for uniform belief, costly commitment, martyrdom traditions, and the movement's expansion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between divine ability to resurrect and historical evidence that a resurrection actually occurred.
Identify pre-Christian or ancient structural parallels that weaken an inference from narrative uniqueness to historical occurrence.

sections.title: Historical method and extraordinary-event inference
sections.rationale: The motion requires an inference from ancient reports to an extraordinary event, making the governing historical standard and the evidential role of early reports foundational to both routes.

sections.title: Meaning of bodily and spiritual resurrection language
sections.rationale: Whether the earliest resurrection language describes transformed physical continuity or an immaterial spiritual condition bears directly on the bodily qualification in the motion.

sections.title: Provenance and coherence of Pauline testimony
sections.rationale: Pauline material is among the earliest evidence invoked, so whether its received and revealed formulations are coherent materially affects the historical foundation of the resurrection claim.

sections.title: Chronology and relevance of pagan resurrection analogues
sections.rationale: The presence or absence of earlier comparable dying-and-rising traditions affects whether the Christian accounts are treated as historically distinctive testimony or as familiar religious narrative forms.

sections.title: Independence and reliability of apostolic transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of later Christian agreement depends on whether it preserves independently grounded apostolic information or merely repeats contested attributions and normative inherited teaching.

sections.title: Martyrdom, costly commitment, and movement growth
sections.rationale: Claims about suffering and expansion can support the sincerity or origins of resurrection belief only if their historical basis and explanatory connection to the event are established.
